checkpoints: Keep ONE combined store rather than four separate stores.
The reason is that separate stores would lose a single Devtools timeline, cross-domain atomic writes, and shared middleware in one move.
Each domain (user, cart, browse, theme) is its own slice factory (a StateCreator) that colocates that domain's state and actions and can be unit-tested alone with fake set/get.

The combined type is an intersection (AppState = UserSlice & CartSlice & BrowseSlice & ThemeSlice) built via the curried create<AppState>()(...) pattern so each factory's set/get is typed against the full state.
A slice's action can read another domain's state through get() (e.g. cart's checkout reading get().user) without importing that other slice's file.
The code-review rule for cross-slice access is: read another domain only via get(), never import another slice's module directly.

Devtools/persist middleware wraps exactly once around the combined creator, not per-slice, because middleware needs the merged state to snapshot or persist correctly; partialize persists only user and theme.
Field names use a domain prefix (cartItems, userLoading, browseFilters, themeMode) so a later slice can't silently overwrite an earlier slice's field on spread.
The atom graph splits into three layers: source, derived, and async.
Source atoms are primitive filter atoms declared at module scope, never created inside a component body, so state persists across renders instead of resetting.
Derived atoms are read-only atoms shaped atom((get) => ...) (e.g. activeFilterCountAtom, hasResultsAtom) that Jotai recomputes only when the specific atoms they read from change.
Because the derived value is computed at the atom level, every component reading it shares the same result, unlike useMemo which caches per component.

The async atom (searchResultsAtom) also reads the filter atoms via get(), so a filter change invalidates and re-runs its fetch producer, and a component reading it via useAtomValue automatically re-suspends, replacing a hand-written useEffect plus loading flag.

The Suspense boundary is placed around the specific component reading searchResultsAtom (e.g. inside ResultsList), not at the route root, so only that region shows a fallback instead of blanking the whole page.
For Object.is dedupe to work, the derived atoms must return primitive values (number/boolean); returning a new object or array each time is always seen as changed and triggers a redundant notify.
Wrapping the comparison modal's subtree in a <Provider> creates a separate child store, so the same atom declarations get a fresh instance and filters never leak between the modal and the page.
Surviving reload and syncing across tabs are two separate problems that need two separate mechanisms, not one 'call setItem in every action' fix.
Wrapping the store with persist and a storage adapter makes every set() write through to storage automatically, with no hand-written setItem call inside any action.
On remount, including after F5, persist rehydrates the store's state from what's already in storage.
Tab sync is solved by having the storage adapter's setItem also broadcast the change (e.g. via BroadcastChannel/postMessage) to other tabs.
Other tabs rehydrate their own state from that broadcast message rather than replaying the action, to avoid an echo loop.
The 'just setItem in every action' approach is fragile because it's easy to forget when a new action is added, silently creating a bug.
That naive approach also fails to sync tabs (nothing tells another tab to broadcast) and fails to rehydrate on reload (nothing re-reads storage when the store initializes).
A newly opened tab can read localStorage directly at mount for an immediate correct value, but the very first frame can still flash the in-memory default before persist.hasHydrated() resolves.

The checkout action is defined inside one slice creator of the combined store (e.g. the cart slice) and receives (set, get) as its creator's own arguments — it is not a standalone function living outside the store.

It reads the other slice by calling get() inside the action body; get() returns the entire combined AppState, not just the current slice's own piece, because the creator is typed StateCreator<AppState, [], [], ThisSlice> (the first generic is the full app state).
It rejects importing another slice's module directly into the action, calling out the cross-file coupling and the circular-dependency risk once that other slice needs to call back.
The cross-domain write is exactly ONE set() call that patches fields from both domains together (e.g. clearing cart items and updating user info in the same call) — not two separate set() calls.

It explains why atomicity is impossible with two separate create() stores: the two writes need two sequential set() calls, and a render can land in the gap between them, exposing a half-updated state (e.g. cart already cleared but user not yet updated, or the reverse).
It names at least one further downside of separate stores beyond atomicity — e.g. two disjoint Devtools timelines, or reconfiguring persist/devtools middleware separately per store instead of once.

It notes that after the cross-slice set(), an unrelated selector (e.g. theme) still skips re-render via Object.is because its own slice's value did not change — isolation holds even though the write touched two other slices.
The storage event only fires in tabs OTHER than the one that wrote — the writing tab itself never receives its own event.
BroadcastChannel has no such gap: postMessage fires on every listener registered on the channel, including the tab that just called postMessage, so one handler can both emit and receive.
The storage event carries only a string (the key's new value) — sending a complex object means hand-rolling JSON.stringify/parse and losing types like Map, Date, and undefined.
BroadcastChannel messages use the structured-clone algorithm, so Maps/Dates/Sets and nested objects keep their real types across the tab boundary.

BroadcastChannel is purpose-built for same-origin cross-context messaging with a simpler API than the storage event (a side effect of the storage API, not a genuine messaging API), and needs no polyfill in evergreen browsers.

BroadcastChannel is still only same-origin and same browser profile on the same machine — a different browser, profile, incognito session, or device hears nothing, even under the same logged-in account.
Real cross-device sync (e.g. phone and laptop) has to push state through a channel with a server in the middle, like WebSocket or SSE, because BroadcastChannel never reaches that far.

Architecturally, BroadcastChannel belongs inside the StateStorage adapter — emit inside setItem, listen via subscribeBroadcast — so the store and UI only ever see a plain storage backend, unaware any sync mechanism is running.
Splitting into separate create() stores loses a single Devtools timeline — each store now has its own disjoint timeline, making an action touching several domains hard to trace.
It also loses cross-slice atomic writes — one set() can no longer patch two domains in the same write, forcing several non-atomic sets that expose intermediate state to the UI.
It loses shared middleware — persist/devtools/immer must be declared separately per store instead of wrapped once around the combined creator.

The slices pattern solves the actual underlying problem (30+ hard-to-manage fields, constant merge conflicts) without paying those costs by keeping exactly ONE store and separating concerns only at the file level.
Each slice is an independent StateCreator factory, written, reviewed, and unit-tested on its own with fake set/get, then spread-merged into one store typed as the intersection of all slices.

The combined store forces namespacing discipline: two slices declaring the same key silently overwrite each other on spread (the later one wins) with no compile error, so fields need domain-qualified names.

Steel-manning separate stores: they're reasonable when two domains genuinely never need to write together in one action and nobody needs to trace them on one shared timeline, e.g. a fully split-off internal dashboard.

When domains live on the same page, need atomic writes together, and get debugged on one shared timeline, the slices pattern is the right answer, not multiple stores — crossing 30+ fields alone doesn't force a split.

Frames the decision by the SHAPE of the state, not personal preference: the settings dashboard (a few independent domain records — user, cart, theme) fits Zustand's one-store/one-update-timeline model; the data-exploration screen (interdependent derived values, per-item state, filter-keyed async data) fits Jotai's graph model.

Describes Jotai's dependency mechanism: a derived atom reads other atoms via get(), so Jotai tracks that as a dependency edge and recomputes the derived atom when the dependency changes, deduping with Object.is; per-item state maps directly onto atomFamily.

Explains the async-atom mechanism: an async atom's producer reads its dependency via get() and returns a Promise, so when the dependency (e.g. the filter) changes, the producer re-runs and the reading component re-suspends through Suspense — no useEffect, no hand-written loading boolean.

Names the concrete race condition the manual useEffect + loading approach hits when the filter changes faster than the previous request resolves — a stale response can arrive later and clobber a fresher one, forcing a hand-rolled AbortController/cancellation flag — and states that Jotai avoids this because it serializes producer re-runs along the dependency graph.
States the cost that atoms must be declared at module scope, since an atom created inline during render is a fresh atom every render and loses its state.
States the cost that a Suspense boundary must wrap exactly the smallest unit that should show a local loader, or the whole route suspends instead of just the failing piece.
States the cost that a derived atom returning a new object or array on every recomputation is always seen as 'changed', because Object.is compares by reference identity, not deep equality.

Gives a mixing policy: both libraries are Provider-less and can technically coexist in one app, but mixing the two models within the SAME feature/flow should be refused, since it forces every reader to switch between 'state is an object' and 'state is a graph'.
The root cause is that CountBadge reads the store with useCounterStore.getState().count during render — getState() is a snapshot read that registers NO subscription whatsoever.
This is unlike calling the hook useCounterStore(selector), which is built on useSyncExternalStore and actually registers the component with the store.
Because no selector is ever registered, no Object.is comparison ever runs for this component when the store changes, so Zustand has no way to know it should notify CountBadge to re-render.

This explains the symptom: the badge only shows the right number when some unrelated cause forces its parent to re-render, at which point getState() is called again and happens to read the latest value, creating the illusion it sometimes updates on its own.
The fix is to change it to const count = useCounterStore((s) => s.count) in render — the hook with a selector IS the subscription.
getState()/get() still has a legitimate use, but only inside an action or event handler for a one-time read at call time — never to source a value displayed in JSX.
Verification: write a test that mutates the store from OUTSIDE CountBadge (call increment() directly, or click a button on another component) and assert the badge's text updates to the new value.
The getState() version fails this test deterministically because the DOM never updates on its own, while the hook-with-selector version passes.
Root cause: the delete/reset branch calls the reset() store ACTION instead of applying state silently, unlike the other branches.
Tab 1's reset click trace: the reset action runs set({ count: 0 }) -> the adapter's setItem -> postMessage on the BroadcastChannel.
Tab 2's attachCrossTabSync receives that message, sees msg.value === null, and calls useCounterStore.getState().reset(), which itself runs its own set() -> setItem -> postMessage back to tab 1.
Tab 1's handler fires again on that echoed null message and calls reset() again, so the two tabs ping-pong forever, each write triggering the other's handler.
The non-null branch never has this problem because useCounterStore.persist.rehydrate() only RE-READS the already-updated localStorage entry, with no set(), no setItem, and no broadcast.

Invariant to keep: a broadcast receiver must never invoke a normal action, because every action's set() re-enters the write-through adapter; when a receiver needs to merge rather than fully rehydrate, keep the invariant alive with a senderId (ignore own messages) or an isApplyingRemote flag.
Fix: make the receiver's delete branch just as silent as the other one via useCounterStore.setState({ count: 0 }) instead of calling reset().

Test that would have caught it: a Playwright test opening two pages in one BrowserContext, clicking reset in tab 1, asserting both tabs converge to count === 0, and asserting the channel's message count stays bounded rather than climbing (a serial single-tab test structurally cannot observe the echo loop).

Most severe (correctness): localCountAtom = atom(0) is declared inside StatsCard's body, so any re-render for an unrelated reason (e.g. a parent prop changing) creates a brand-new atom instance and count silently resets to 0 with no exception thrown.

Fix for the atom-scope bug: declare localCountAtom at module scope alongside the other atoms in lib/atoms.ts, or, if a genuinely per-instance local atom is needed, use useMemo(() => atom(0), []) so it's only ever created once.

Moderately severe (UX): asyncStatsAtom reads filterAtom, so every filter change re-runs the async producer and re-suspends the component reading it; since the nearest Suspense boundary in the whole route sits at the root, the suspension unwinds all the way up there and blanks the ENTIRE page.

Fix for the Suspense bug: split the part reading asyncStatsAtom into an inner component and wrap it with a local <Suspense fallback> right inside StatsCard, so the fallback only shows locally inside the card.

Lighter code-smell finding: StatsLabel uses useAtom(labelAtom) despite only reading it and importing a setter it never calls; switch to useAtomValue(labelAtom) to keep the subscription footprint small and match the read-only intent.
Verification for the reset bug: re-render the parent component for a reason unrelated to count and assert count keeps its previous value — this test fails against the inline-atom version.

Verification for the Suspense bug: change the filter and assert only the card's local loading testid appears while the rest of the page chrome (header, nav, other cards) stays visible — this test fails if the local Suspense boundary is missing.
